# Attadaṇḍa Sutta (Snp 4.15 (PTS Snp 182))

**ID:** Snp 4.15 (PTS Snp 182)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Attadaṇḍa Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Taking Up Arms
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp4.15
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Attadaṇḍa Sutta* is the fifteenth discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 4.15, starting at verse 935) [Anderson and Smith 1913; Segall 2003]. In an *uddāna* verse it is alternatively designated as *Attadaṇḍavara* [Norman 1997–2001]. In English it has been titled "Taking Up Arms" [SuttaCentral] and "The Use of Violence" [Nyanaponika 1978]. Opening with the striking declaration that fear arises from taking up weapons or violence (*attadaṇḍā bhayam jātam*) and observing people embroiled in strife, the Buddha recounts the profound spiritual shock (*saṁvega*) that prompted him to renounce household life [Anderson and Smith 1913; Nyanaponika 1978; SuttaCentral]. He concludes with instructions on practice and a description of one who has attained genuine peace and security [SuttaCentral]. Commentarial tradition, as in the Mahāniddesa and the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, glosses *attadaṇḍa* as one's own misconduct, though philologically it signifies an uplifted stick or weapon [Norman 1997–2001]. While modern scholars view the sutta as an archaic, realistic account of the Buddha's impetus toward renunciation [Anālayo 2017; Sujato 2011], post-canonical narrative traditions, such as the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, frame it as a sermon preached by the Buddha to quell the armed water dispute on the Rohiṇī River between the Sākyas and Koliyas [Fausböll 1891; Goyal 2003; Kwee 2015].

A full Chinese parallel is preserved in the *Yizu jing* (T 198) [Anālayo 2017; SuttaCentral]. Individual verse parallels exist across Dharmapada and Udānavarga traditions, including Dhammapada 367, the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (G-Dhp), several Chinese Dharmapada recensions (T 210, T 212, T 213), and Sanskrit and Tibetan recensions of the *Udānavarga* (UV 32, D4099) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, the entire text is explicated in the canonical *Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 15) [SuttaCentral; Sujin Boriharnwanaket], which shares 90 passages of extensive text reuse with this discourse in DharmaNexus match data, alongside shared segments in the *Cullaniddesa* (Cnd 15) and later aṭṭhakathā literature [DharmaNexus].
